corrections.why: The standing cast-iron tower is the 1926 reconstruction; the 1908 tower was a wooden hexagonal frame tower dismantled in 1926.
Lighthousefriends and the Delaware state marker date the first (temporary) lights to 1 January 1902; the USLHS archive says established 1901.
The foundation's website says tours are suspended at the Army Corps of Engineers' request; the tower is offshore.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: 1901 is the USLHS establishment year and the date the breakwater was finished; the first lights were temporary, shown 1 January 1902; the 1908 tower was the first permanent lighthouse; the present tower relit 15 November 1926.
The 1908 light flashed white every 12 seconds per Lighthousefriends quoting the Light-House Board; the 1926 light gave one flash every 10 seconds per the 1928 Bulletin.

notes_for_editor: Not found: annual reports for fiscal 1902-1914 (Light-House Board volumes for those years are not in the corpus), so the 1908 construction details (cost $49,941, 20 Nov 1908, 12-second flash, 40-ft concrete block, wooden superstructure and the $20,000 of 1906) rest on Lighthousefriends, which says it quotes the Light-House Board; the 1903 storm damage to the temporary lights and Marshall's report likewise rest on Lighthousefriends alone. The Hattie A. Marsh details are from the Daily Kennebec Journal of 17 Sept 1903 p. 1 (OCR page read through newspapers.py); the Washington Times of the same date spells the captain Mahaffy; Lighthousefriends spells him Mehaffey and gives a different place for the wreck (against the breakwater) than the newspaper's 'rocks of the harbor of refuge'. Disagreements flagged in the story: first-light year 1901 vs 1902; replacement vs reconstruction in 1926 (the 1928 Bulletin says the station was reconstructed and 'remodeled'; whether the 1908 iron foundation was reused is not stated); NRHP says the lights were manned until the 1950s while the roster lists Coast Guard crews 1959-1973 and Lighthousefriends/Delaware marker say automation was December 1973; Lighthousefriends says tours reopened in 2018 but the foundation's own site now says no tours at Army Corps' request. The USLHS place record lists the current optic as a DCB-36 (solar powered) while Lighthousefriends and the Chesapeake Chapter say a Vega VRB-25 replaced it in 1996. Names matched by roster position: none from OCR tables; the keeper roster is the USLHS list as printed. Variants: Hickman is George H. (roster, Bulletin 1920 p. 12) and George C. (Bulletin 1920 p. 9 and index); Schmierer is Schierer in the Bulletin of Sept 1920; Taylor is printed Robert L. once. The 1920 Bulletin page 9 and 12 pages were read from the PDF text where columns interleave, so the quoted fragments are the contiguous ones. Bulletin 1930 item (July 12 rescue) does not give the year inside the item; it appears in the 1930 volume. Bulletin 1924-29 index lists 'Taylor, Robert C., keeper Harbor of Refuge, at Philadelphia Exposition' (p. 174) which was not followed up. Coast Guard crewmen after 1960 are not named in the story except Angelo Rigazio, who is named publicly by Lighthousefriends as a later association president.
